hints: Ask yourself which structure penicillin attacks in bacteria but is completely missing from your own human cells, that is why it is safe for us.
Remember how a competitive inhibitor works by shape similarity, blocking the active site of the transpeptidase enzyme that cross-links the bacterial wall.
walkthrough:
**Start with what makes bacteria vulnerable**

Bacteria are surrounded by a peptidoglycan cell wall. Human cells do not have this wall at all.

That is a perfect antibiotic target, because you can damage bacteria without harming human cells.

**Recall how penicillin blocks the wall enzyme**

Penicillin has a shape very similar to the normal substrate of the enzyme transpeptidase.

It fits into the active site and blocks it, so it acts as a competitive inhibitor. Without this enzyme, new cross-links cannot form and the wall becomes weak.

**Link weak wall to bacterial death**

When bacteria grow and divide, a weak wall cannot withstand water entering by osmosis.

The cell swells and bursts, so penicillin is bactericidal. That points clearly to option C.

options.A: Penicillin does not bind nucleotides or stop DNA replication, that is the action of some other antibiotics like quinolones.
options.B: Blocking tRNA binding to ribosomes describes antibiotics that stop translation, such as tetracycline, not penicillin.
options.C: Correct. Penicillin is a competitive inhibitor of transpeptidase, preventing peptidoglycan cross-linking in cell wall synthesis.
options.D: Penicillin does not inhibit protein synthesis enzymes, it is specific to the cell wall building enzyme.
